V01-B-001: Each generation of naturalists tends to take the abundance of wildlife it first encountered as the natural state of things. When numbers fall during their working lives, they record the loss against that starting point rather than against any earlier one. Their successors, beginning from the depleted world that those records describe, then treat the reduced numbers as normal in turn. Over several generations, this quiet resetting of expectations allows a dramatic decline to pass almost unnoticed, since no one remembers the earlier abundance.
V01-B-002: A company that pays for trees to be planted can claim that its emissions have been offset by the carbon those trees absorb. The claim assumes, however, that the carbon will stay locked away for as long as the emitted carbon dioxide remains in the atmosphere, which may be centuries. A forest offers no such guarantee: it can burn, be felled when land prices change, or die back in a drought. If any of these happens, the stored carbon returns to the air, and the emission that was supposedly cancelled turns out only to have been postponed. An offset, then, should be judged not by how much carbon it captures in its first years but by how confident we can be that the carbon will stay captured.
V01-B-003: Rivers and lakes that are shrinking can be seen, photographed and argued over, which is one reason their decline draws public attention. Groundwater enjoys no such visibility, since it lies in rock and gravel beneath the very fields that draw on it. As a result, an aquifer can be pumped faster than rain refills it for decades before anyone notices, usually when wells must be drilled ever deeper. By the time that happens, the water lost may have taken thousands of years to accumulate and cannot be replaced within any human lifetime.
V01-B-004: Complaints about light pollution are often dismissed as the special pleading of astronomers, a small group whose instruments are troubled by the glow of cities. Professional observatories, though, have largely solved their problem by moving to remote mountains, so they are not the ones who lose most. The real losers are the millions of city dwellers who have never seen the Milky Way and do not know what has been taken from them. That ignorance is precisely what keeps the complaint marginal, since a loss nobody remembers is a loss nobody demands back.
V01-B-005: Rules that require every password to contain a capital letter, a digit and a symbol are meant to make passwords harder to guess. Faced with such demands, most people do the least the rules allow, capitalising the first letter and adding a digit and an exclamation mark at the end. Because so many users follow the same pattern, attackers simply build it into their guessing programs, and the extra characters add far less protection than their number suggests. Against such programs, a long phrase of ordinary words, which the rules may even reject, can be stronger than the predictable short password they end up producing.
V01-B-006: Programmers speak of 'technical debt' when a team ships a quick fix instead of the careful solution it knows it should build. Like a loan, the shortcut brings an immediate benefit, because the feature reaches users weeks earlier than it otherwise would. Also like a loan, it charges interest: every later change has to work around the hasty code and so takes longer than it should. Unless the team eventually sets aside time to rewrite that code, the interest can grow until most of its effort goes into servicing old shortcuts.
V01-B-007: It is often said that a familiar keyboard layout survives only because of lock-in: everyone learned it, so no one can afford to abandon it. The argument has a real logic, since a typist who retrains alone pays the full cost of switching while gaining little until offices, schools and manufacturers switch too. Even granting this, the argument rests on a premise that is rarely examined, namely that a clearly better layout exists and is being passed over. If careful trials showed the supposed improvement to be marginal, the old layout's survival would need no special explanation at all. So lock-in can explain why an inferior standard persists, but whether the standard is inferior is a separate question that only such trials can settle.
V01-B-008: Drivers considering an electric car often ask first how far it can go on a single charge. The question is natural, yet most of them drive only a short distance on a typical day, far less than even a modest battery provides. What they are really insuring against is the rare long journey, the holiday drive or the emergency trip, on which running out of charge would be a serious problem. For that reason, a dense network of fast chargers along major roads may reassure buyers more than any increase in battery size.
V01-B-009: A narrator who misreports events might seem to be a defect in a novel, since readers depend on the teller for everything they learn. Yet some of the most admired fiction is built on exactly such a teller, whose account the reader gradually learns to distrust. The pleasure lies in reading through the narration to what it conceals, noticing a detail the narrator mentions but fails to understand. This kind of reading is possible, however, only if the author has planted enough clues for the gap between account and event to be detected. A narrator who deceives the reader completely, leaving no such clues, produces not irony but merely a trick revealed on the last page.
V01-B-010: When a painting long admired as a master's work is exposed as a forgery, its price collapses, even though not a single brushstroke has changed. This can look like snobbery, as if buyers had been paying for a signature rather than for anything they could see. The charge misses something, for a painting is admired not only as a surface but also as an achievement, the solution an artist found to problems of a particular time. A copy made later, by someone who already knew the solution, reproduces the look of that achievement without being one, and it is the achievement whose loss the price records.
V01-B-011: Readers often complain that a film has betrayed the novel on which it was based. The complaint usually assumes that a good adaptation should include as much of the book as possible. That assumption, however, ignores the form, since a two-hour film cannot hold all the incidents of a long novel; cutting is not betrayal but a condition of film. The fairer test is therefore whether the film keeps the spirit of the book, not whether it keeps its scenes.
V01-B-012: Cleaning an old painting seems a straightforward good: centuries of grime and yellowed varnish are removed, and the colours the artist chose appear again. The difficulty is that some of what looks like dirt may be the artist's own work, a thin tinted glaze laid over the paint to soften it. Since such glazes and later varnish can be chemically similar, a restorer may remove both together without realising it. The brighter picture that results can then be less faithful than the dim one it replaced, however much it pleases the eye.
V01-B-013: Campaigns to keep a language pure usually target words borrowed from other languages. Yet almost every language has absorbed foreign words for centuries, often so thoroughly that its speakers no longer recognise them as borrowed. Many of the words that purists defend as native were themselves once newcomers, adopted from traders, conquerors or neighbours. If even the purists' own vocabulary was once borrowed, a pure language is not something that has been lost but something that has never existed.
V01-B-014: A headline phrased as a question, such as one asking whether a common food causes illness, lets a publication raise a frightening possibility without asserting it. If the article finds no good evidence, the publication can still say that it merely asked, and no one can accuse it of having made a false claim. Readers are not protected in the same way, since they tend to remember the possibility the headline raised rather than the doubt in its grammar. That grammatical doubt thus shields the writer without reaching the reader, who leaves with an impression the article itself may not support.
V01-B-015: A polite term is often introduced to replace a word that has come to sound insulting when applied to some condition or group. For a while the new term works, because it carries none of the contempt that had gathered around the old one. But the contempt was never in the old word's sounds; it lay in attitudes towards the people the word described. As long as those attitudes persist, they attach themselves to the replacement, which in time sounds as harsh as the word it displaced. Renaming can signal respect, then, but it cannot by itself produce the change in attitude on which its success depends.
V01-B-016: Many people consult a dictionary to find out how a word ought to be used, as if it were a rulebook. Most modern dictionary makers, by contrast, see their task as recording how words are actually used by speakers and writers. When enough people use a word in a new sense, they add that sense, even if it began as what older speakers regard as an error. Readers who expected a rulebook then accuse the dictionary of approving mistakes. The accusation misreads the dictionary's purpose, much as one might blame a map for showing a road that the mapmaker thinks should never have been built.
V01-B-017: When most students in a course receive top grades, the grade stops distinguishing the excellent from the merely competent. Employers and admissions officers, unable to learn much from the grade, begin to rely on other signals, such as the reputation of the institution. Those signals favour students who attended well-known schools, whatever their individual ability. Generous grading, intended as kindness to students, can thus end up penalising the able student from an obscure school, whose top grade no longer stands out.
V01-B-018: Students preparing for an exam often reread their notes, since the material feels more familiar each time. That feeling of familiarity, however, is a poor guide to whether they will be able to recall the material without the notes in front of them. Testing oneself without the notes is harder and less pleasant, but it practises exactly that act of recall, the one the exam will demand. The more effective method is thus the one that feels less productive while it is being used.
V01-B-019: Reducing class sizes seems an obvious way to improve teaching, since each pupil can receive more of the teacher's attention. That benefit depends, though, on teachers changing how they teach, for a lecture delivered to twenty pupils differs little from one delivered to thirty-five. Even where teachers do adapt, a policy that cuts class sizes across a whole country must find many more teachers at once, and the new recruits may be less experienced than those already employed. The gain from smaller classes can therefore be smaller than expected, or can disappear altogether, when the reform is made too quickly and on too large a scale.
V01-B-020: Teachers who return written work with both a mark and detailed comments often find that pupils look at the mark and ignore the rest. The mark, once seen, settles the question most pupils care about, which is how they did compared with their classmates. Since that question cannot be answered from a page with no mark on it, some schools have experimented with returning comments alone, at least for drafts. The approach asks a great deal of teachers, however, since comments that are vague or generic give pupils nothing worth reading in place of the mark.
V01-B-021: Rote memorisation is often contrasted unfavourably with understanding, as if the two competed for a pupil's time. Understanding a topic, however, largely consists in seeing how facts connect, and facts that are not held in memory cannot be connected. A pupil who must look up every date while reading about a historical period has no attention left for noticing which events caused which. None of this means that memorised facts amount to understanding, and a pupil who could recite every date might still miss what links them. Memory and understanding are thus partners rather than rivals: memorised facts are the material, and understanding is the work that, as the reciting pupil shows, must still be done on them.
V01-B-022: Screening healthy people for cancer seems an unmixed good, since a tumour found early is usually easier to treat. Some tumours that screening finds, however, grow so slowly that they would never have caused symptoms in the patient's lifetime. Because doctors cannot always tell such tumours from dangerous ones, many of them are treated anyway, with surgery or radiation that carries its own harms. Those who come through the treatment, as nearly all such patients do, are then counted among the successes of screening, which makes the programme look better than it is. A rise in the number of cancers detected and survived is therefore not, on its own, evidence that screening is saving lives.
V01-B-023: Hospitals have long known that cleaning hands between patients is one of the simplest ways to prevent infections from spreading. Even so, staff often skip it, not out of carelessness but because a busy shift may call for cleaning their hands dozens of times. Placing alcohol rub dispensers at every bedside reduces this burden, since cleaning hands then takes seconds rather than a walk to a sink. The lesson is that compliance often depends less on exhorting staff than on making the right action easy.
V01-B-024: A fever is usually treated as part of the illness, something to be brought down as quickly as possible. In many infections, however, the raised temperature is the body's own response, and it may help the immune system while slowing the growth of some pathogens. If so, routinely suppressing a moderate fever could in some cases lengthen the very illness it seems to relieve. This does not mean that fevers should simply be left alone, since very high temperatures are dangerous in themselves, but it does suggest that comfort and cure are not always the same goal.
V01-B-025: Many people treat sleep as an account they can overdraw during the week and repay at the weekend. A night of short sleep does leave a debt of sorts, felt as drowsiness and slower reactions the next day. One long lie-in, however, does not seem to repay several such nights in full, since some of the impairment persists. The second problem is harder to notice: people who are chronically short of sleep often underestimate how impaired they are, because the tiredness comes to feel normal. The weekend repayment plan therefore fails twice, since it does not fully restore performance and it relies on a judgement that the debt itself has distorted.
